title: Why Nobody Can Afford a House Anymore

scenes.narration: Owning a home used to be the most ordinary thing in the world. Get a job, save for a few years, and the keys were yours.
Your parents probably did it in their twenties. Maybe on a single income — on a salary that today sounds like a typo.
For a whole generation, that deal is just gone. The house is still standing right there. The door just won't open for you.
The typical American home now costs more than four hundred thousand dollars. A brand-new record.
To get a loan that size, a bank wants to see you earning around a hundred and twenty-seven thousand dollars a year.
The problem? The typical American household earns about eighty thousand. The math quietly stopped working.
And the starter home — the small, cheap, first place you actually buy — has basically gone extinct.
Here's the comparison that stings. In the nineteen-eighties, a typical home cost about two to three years of a typical salary.
Today, that same ordinary house costs the better part of a decade of income — before a single cent of interest.
Same four walls. A completely different mountain to climb.
And this isn't envy, and it isn't avocado toast. A whole generation is playing a game where the rules changed halfway through the round.
So everyone reaches for a villain. Greedy landlords. Wall Street. Boomers. Foreigners. Airbnb. Take your pick.
But blaming one villain is exactly why nothing ever gets fixed. The real story isn't a person. It's four charts.
And once you've actually seen these four, you will never look at a 'For Sale' sign the same way again.
So let's follow the money — right up to the front door.
scenes.heading: Why Nobody Can Afford a House

scenes.narration: Chart one. The gap between what a house costs and what a human being actually earns.
For most of modern history, a typical home cost about three times a year's income. Expensive — but reachable.
You could save a down payment in a few years and grow into the mortgage. The ladder actually had rungs.
Today, the typical home costs five times income — tying the most expensive level ever recorded.
scenes.title: U.S. home price ÷ household income

scenes.narration: And this isn't a vibe. Harvard's housing center clocked the national price-to-income ratio at a record five-point-zero.
Here's the engine behind that line. Two things that were supposed to move together — and completely came apart.
Home prices went nearly vertical. And wages? Wages basically crawled along the floor.
When the thing you're buying triples while your paycheck barely moves, that's not a budgeting problem. It's a math problem.
So why did prices run away like this? A few fires, all lit at once.
A giant generation — millennials — all hit home-buying age at the same moment, flooding the market with buyers.
A decade of ultra-cheap borrowing let every one of them bid higher without feeling it — until the bill finally came due.
And a home quietly became a savings account. If prices only ever go up, buying early stops feeling like a purchase and starts feeling like a bet you can't lose.
Zillow's own index tells the same story — the typical home value roughly doubled in well under a decade.
In 2021, one in three renters could still afford the typical home. Two years later, it was one in seven.
scenes.sub: renters who can afford a median home

scenes.narration: The ladder didn't just get taller. Somebody came along and sawed off the bottom rungs.
And the cruel twist: people who bought in early watched their house out-earn their actual job.
And it compounds against you. Every year you can't buy, prices climb again — and the down payment you were chasing sprints further away.
But the sticker price hides half the story. Almost nobody pays cash. You don't buy the price — you buy the monthly payment.
And here's the part the brochure never explains. In the early years of a thirty-year loan, almost every dollar you pay is pure interest.
You're not really buying the house yet. You're renting the bank's money — and the rent on money is the interest rate.
And that payment is ruled by one number that has nothing to do with the house itself. Chart two: the interest rate.
In the pandemic, the Fed pinned rates to the floor. Mortgages dropped below three percent. Borrowing was almost free.
Sounds great. But when everyone can suddenly borrow more, they all bid more — and prices leap up to swallow the cheap money.
Then inflation hit, and in barely eighteen months, mortgage rates nearly touched eight percent — the fastest spike in forty years.
scenes.title: 30-year mortgage rate (%)

scenes.narration: Same house. Same price tag. But the monthly check you write for it roughly doubled.
A payment that was around seventeen hundred a month became nearly three thousand — for the exact same four walls.
That's an extra fifteen thousand dollars a year — forever — for literally nothing new. Same house, same street, same paint.
And before any of that, you need the down payment. Tens of thousands in cash — saved while rent quietly eats a third of every paycheck.
So you're asked to save faster than ever, for a bigger number than ever, out of the paycheck that grew the slowest of all.
And you don't set that rate — the market and the Fed do. This is Freddie Mac's own weekly record of the spike.
Why did rates explode? To fight the worst inflation in forty years, the Fed hiked its own rate hard — and mortgages followed it straight up.
Here's the cruel irony. Cheap rates never really made homes affordable. They just let sellers charge more. The price quietly absorbs every drop in the rate.
So even if prices had frozen solid, the cost of carrying a home still exploded. Two locks on the same front door.
By now you're yelling the obvious fix. Just build more houses. Supply and demand. Chart three.
Right instinct. One problem. For about fifteen years, America quietly stopped building enough of them.
After the 2008 crash, homebuilding fell off a cliff — and unlike the stock market, it never fully climbed back.
scenes.title: New homes built (million / year)

scenes.narration: A whole decade of building too little, while the population kept growing. The hole just got deeper every single year.
Add it all up, and the country is short by nearly four million homes.
And Freddie Mac doesn't treat that as a footnote. It calls the shortage the root cause of the entire affordability crisis.
So why can't we just build? Because a new home hits a wall of rules before a single brick is ever laid.
Zoning that bans anything but big single houses. Expensive land. Pricey labor and materials. Years of permits.
There's also a quieter reason. When building anything is this hard, builders only bother with the homes that earn the fattest margin.
So they build the five-bedroom, not the starter. The cheap first home is the exact one almost nobody builds anymore.
And the 2008 crash wiped out thousands of small local builders. The ones left standing are big, cautious, and slow.
And then the neighbors. The people who already own show up to every meeting to block anything new nearby.
They vote to protect their view and their home value over your chance to ever have one. Quietly, it works.
We also quietly outlawed the in-between. Duplexes, townhouses, small apartment blocks — the 'missing middle' that used to be the affordable rung.
In the hottest cities the result is brutal: the nurse and the teacher can no longer afford to live anywhere near the people they serve.
So we took the one fix that genuinely works — more homes — and made it the single hardest thing in America to do.
And every missing home is a bidding war that never had to happen — a family that could've just had a key, fighting over scraps instead.
And here's the twist that quietly makes all of it worse. Chart four. Even the homes that already exist aren't for sale.
Remember those below-three-percent pandemic mortgages? Roughly half of all homeowners are still holding one.
Now picture their choice. Sell this house, and your next mortgage is at seven percent — often on a smaller place.
Your payment could actually go UP just to downsize. So rational people do the only sane thing. They stay put.
There's a name for it. Golden handcuffs. Your old rate is so good it quietly traps you in a house you've already outgrown.
A family with a three-percent loan would pay thousands more a year to buy the identical house next door at seven. So nobody moves.
The result shows up instantly in the data. The number of homes for sale dried up — frozen near record lows.
scenes.title: Homes for sale (million)

scenes.narration: Economists estimate this lock-in froze roughly one-point-seven million home sales in just two years.
And here's the sting. By choking supply even further, the FHFA found lock-in pushed prices up by about another seven percent.
It's a doom loop. Nothing's for sale, so the few buyers left fight over scraps — and bid each other up.
With resale frozen, brand-new homes became almost the only ones for sale — and builders know it, so they almost never have to cut the price.
It's the cruelest kind of trap. The people most stuck are the ones who did everything right and locked in a great rate.
So with almost nothing on the market, ask the real question. Who actually wins a bidding war?
Not the family with a mortgage and a home inspection. The winner is whoever can skip all of that — and pay cash.
Which is increasingly Wall Street. In recent years, investors bought roughly one in four of the cheapest homes in America.
And this isn't a conspiracy — the purchase data is public. Big investors simply became the buyer nobody could outbid.
They don't need a loan, an inspection, or a good night's sleep. They offer cash, today, over asking.
Some firms stopped waiting entirely. They now build whole neighborhoods designed never to be sold — only rented, forever.
So the starter home didn't just get expensive. For a lot of families, it quietly turned into a rental they'll pay on for life.
And once a few big players own enough rentals, they can lean on the same software to set the rent — nudging prices up in lockstep.
A young couple finally saves a down payment, finds the one, writes the offer — and loses before lunch to a company they'll never meet.
And the people locked out of buying don't vanish. They rent. And rents climbed right alongside the prices.
A record twenty-two million renter households now spend more than a third of their income just to keep a roof overhead.
scenes.sub: renters stretched thin by housing costs

scenes.narration: Harvard tracks that number too, and it keeps breaking its own record — more renters stretched thinner every year.
So life goes on hold. People move back in with parents. They delay the move, the wedding, the kid.
And it splits a whole generation in two — not by income, but by timing. Did you buy before the door shut, or after?
For the first time in modern memory, young adults are statistically less likely to own a home than their parents were at the same age.
And the gap compounds every year. Owners watched their equity balloon while they slept.
Renters paid an entire mortgage every month — just somebody else's. One side quietly builds wealth. The other builds it for a landlord.
And rent isn't building you anything. Thirty years of rent checks, and you end with exactly what you started with — a stack of receipts.
Picture it. You did everything right — a degree, a steady job, no debt. And the cheapest home near work still needs an income you just don't have.
That's how a housing market quietly turns into a wealth-sorting machine — before you've even bought a thing.
None of this fell from the sky. After World War Two, America bet its whole middle class on one idea: a house, and a thirty-year mortgage.
It worked beautifully — for the people who got in. The home became the family's retirement plan, its inheritance, its everything.
Which is the trap. Once a country stores its wealth inside home prices, letting those prices fall becomes politically unthinkable.
So, the villain. Here's the uncomfortable answer. There isn't one. It's the whole machine, working exactly as designed.
Because somewhere along the way, a house stopped being a place to live. It quietly became an investment.
And an investment has exactly one job. Go up. Every rate cut, every tax break, every rule quietly serves that one job.
Economists even have a word for the force behind it. Homevoters — people who, above all else, vote to protect the value of their home.
So the real fight over housing isn't left versus right. It's the people who already own versus everyone who hasn't bought in yet.
It doesn't have to be this way. A few countries treat housing first as shelter, and build relentlessly to keep it cheap — on purpose.
Which is why every honest fix has a loser. Build four million homes, and you dent the biggest asset most families own.
Cut rates to help buyers, and you just hand everyone a bigger loan — and the price floats right back up.
For the two-thirds of Americans who already own, the system isn't broken at all. It's working perfectly.
And they vote. Which is exactly why the one thing that would help most is the thing that almost never happens.
So no — you are not crazy, and you are not bad with money. The door really did move. The math really did change.
A home became the one thing we all need to live in… and the one thing we quietly decided must never be allowed to get cheaper.
Four charts. Prices up. Rates up. Building down. The market frozen. Stack them together, and the locked door isn't a mystery anymore.
Four charts. Prices up, rates up, building down, and the whole market frozen in place. That's the lock on the door.
And the painful part? A lot of the people with the power to fix it are the exact people the broken version quietly made rich.
If this finally made the numbers click, hit subscribe — and tell me which impossible price you want me to pull apart next.
I do the reading. You get the parts that matter.
